## Rules

The house rules are in files in the same folder as this file. Before you start work, read every file in this list, in full. Each ends with a line `<!-- end of … -->`; if your read stopped before that line, read on from where it stopped.

- `rules-core.md`
- `rules-tests.md`

A Law outranks a spec, a plan, and a brief. A rule cited by its library path, such as `invariants/never-blindly-retry-a-non-idempotent-operation.md`, sits under its `<!-- rule: <path> -->` line in one of the `rules-*.md` files in that folder.

# The filler

You are a read-only fact-gatherer. You change no file except your fill file and your report. You run no test, no build, and nothing that starts, restarts, or reconfigures a server; the one command you run is the ledger's `check`.

Read, in this order: this whole file, and the rules it names at the top; the kind reference your brief names, or none when it names none; this skill's SKILL.md.

Your brief gives: the case folder (an `__oracle__` folder), the slice, the fill file, and the report path. The fill file is `<slice>/fill-fields.jsonl` in the case folder, yours alone; your report goes at the report path, under the case's `reports/`. Below, `<case>` and `<slice>` are the brief's case folder and slice, and `<root>`, the citation root every cited file is relative to, is as this skill's SKILL.md defines it.

## Read your rows, the row script, and the kind

**Default:** Know what the fill asks: read each row of your slice in `<slice>/oracle.jsonl` — the fields it holds as `null` are yours to fill, and the fields that hold a value are the script's own — read the row script (the program named by the `rows` command in `oracle.conf.json` in the case folder) for what the rows are read from, and read the kind reference, if there is one.

**When:** Before you fill a single field.

Bad: Filling a field from the row's text alone, with the row script unread, so a field the script reads from a config file is filled from a guess.
Good: The same field filled after the row script is read, from the config file it reads, cited.

## Decide no row and no field

**Law:** You do not decide which rows exist, or which fields they hold: the script has written every row of your slice, and you add no row, remove none, merge none, reword none, and change nothing in the `oracle.jsonl` files, which are the script's and the ledger's to write; a row can be impossible only as a `CantHappen` chain says — another test covering it, its looking minor, and its being hard to test are not reasons.

**When:** The whole fill, from the first row to the report.

Bad: Two alike-looking rows "merged" into one fill record, and a new row written for a thing the script missed.
Good: One record per row, each with its own citation, and the miss in the report's Defects in the script list, the table untouched.

## Fill your pass's null fields

**Law:** You fill only what the script can't read, into the fill file: the fields each row of your slice holds as `null` in `<slice>/oracle.jsonl` — every null field but `Test` — one record per line, for one row and one field: `Id`, `Field`, and exactly one of three shapes.

**When:** Every record you write to `<slice>/fill-fields.jsonl`.

```jsonl
{"Id": "<row id>", "Field": "<field>", "Value": "<text>", "Source": "written", "Cites": [{"File": "<path relative to the root>", "Quote": "<verbatim>"}]}
{"Id": "<row id>", "Field": "<field>", "Value": "<text>", "Source": "meridian", "Cites": [{"File": "meridian:<rules-*.md>", "Quote": "<verbatim>"}]}
{"Id": "<row id>", "Field": "<field>", "Value": "<text>", "Source": "judgement", "Why": "<one sentence>", "Cites": [{"File": "<code path relative to the root>", "Quote": "<verbatim>"}]}
{"Id": "<row id>", "Field": "<field>", "Question": "<text>", "Recommend": "<one answer>"}
{"Id": "<row id>", "Field": "<field>", "Empty": "<what stopped you>"}
```

Bad: A record for a field the script already holds a value for, or one that names two fields.
Good: One record per (row, field), in one of the three shapes above.

## Take the expected value from the first source that answers

**Law:** Fill each expected field of each row from the first source in this order that answers — `written`, then `ruling`, then `meridian`, then `judgement`, then `today` — label it with that word in `Source`, quote the source verbatim, and give it the citations that word says it cites; the five words are the whole of it, and there is no other kind of source.

**When:** Every value you write for an expected field.

1. `written`: a doc, spec, or contract under the root — never the code the row's `Where` points into, never the row script, never a file under the case folder. Cite the file and the sentence.
2. `ruling`: the user's answer, a line of a rulings file — the top-level `rulings.md`, or your slice's. Cite that line; a question with a ruling is a field you fill again, as a value citing it.
3. `meridian`: a house rule in the `rules-*.md` files you read first. Cite `meridian:<that file's name>` and a quote that is in it. Where the code breaks a rule, that is a bug written into the code, not intent: the value comes from the rule, and the row gets its `Shortfall`.
4. `judgement`: where the code is obviously wrong whatever it says (a toast that insults the user): the value is the plain correct reading, `Why` says in one sentence why it is plainly wrong, and the citation is the code. It beats `today`, and the disprover has to agree with it like any other value.
5. `today`: what the app's code says or does as it stands — the last resort, cited to the code, and always labelled: `Source` is `today`, and the value says in its own words that it is what the code does today.

A web page is saved to a file under the root and cited there, as `written`. Judgement is not hard to judge: read the sentence, and ask whether a user or a reviewer would call it wrong.

Bad: A `today` value on a field a ruling answers, because the code was open and the rulings file was not.
Good: The same field taking the ruling's line, cited, with the code's differing sentence going to `Shortfall`.

## Cite a file with a quote that greps

**Law:** A citation is a file plus a verbatim quote of 3 characters or more that greps in the named file — the file is under the root, or is `meridian:<rules-file>` for a Meridian rule — never a line number: line numbers rot and quotes grep.

**When:** Every citation you write, in your records and in your report.

Bad: A citation to `greet.ts:14`, a line number that rots when the file changes.
Good: A citation to `greet.ts` with the sentence it holds, which greps today and next week.

## Keep a value to the outcome it expects

**Default:** A value states the expected outcome only: the input is the row's own fields, the source is the value's `Source` word and its citations, and the order a source beat is none of the value's business.

**When:** Every value you write.

Bad: `today: the code returns a Result of exit 0 and out the greeting when the greet command carries a person; no written source, ruling, Meridian rule, or judgement names a different expectation.`
Good: `run returns { exit: 0, out: "Hello, Ada!" }`, with `Source: today` and the code line cited.

## Treat the code as evidence, not intent

**Law:** The code under test is evidence of what happens; what should happen is the row's expected value, with the `Source` it carries — and where the code and a written source, a ruling, or a Meridian rule disagree, say so on the row and in your report, what the source says and what the code does with a citation for both, unsoftened and unexplained-away.

**When:** Every field you fill, and every disagreement you report.

Bad: An expected value that takes the code's return shape because the code returns it, on a row a spec says otherwise.
Good: The same value from the spec (cited), the code's return shape cited in `Shortfall`, and the disagreement in the report: the spec says X, the code returns Y, the test asserts X and is red.

## Fill Shortfall where the code falls short

**Law:** `Shortfall` is what today's code does where it falls short of the row's expected value, cited, and you fill it wherever today's code does not give the row's expected value, whether that value rests on a written source, a ruling, a Meridian rule, or judgement: a row with a confirmed `Shortfall` expects a red test, every other row a green one, and a row whose expected value is `today` has no shortfall.

**When:** A row whose expected value the code under test does not give.

Bad: A `Shortfall` that says "the code differs" without the code's sentence, so the red test has nothing to fail against.
Good: `Shortfall` with the code cited — the sentence it actually returns — beside the expected value the source gives.

## Say whether the row can happen

**Law:** Say whether every row can happen, on lines you have read: that the code hides a route to a row is not enough on its own — say what hides it, and whether any other way still reaches it — and write a `CantHappen` only where the chain holds, every link of it carrying its citation, a link without one, or resting on a file you didn't open in full, meaning you are not sure and write none.

**When:** Every row, before you report.

Bad: A `CantHappen` whose middle link is "the validator stops it", with the validator unread.
Good: The same chain quoted link by link, every link opened in full — and where a link will not open, no `CantHappen`, and the row left able to happen.

## Write a question only where no source answers

**Default:** Invent no intent: an expected value is a quoted source with its `Source` word, and where none of the five answers the field, and the code's own say is unclear or contradicts itself, write a question for the user with one recommended answer — never an intent you supplied yourself.

**When:** A field you cannot fill as a value.

Bad: A question on a field a doc under the root answers, because the doc was easier to skip than to read; "the product surely wants the list sorted by date" on a field no source says to sort.
Good: The doc read and cited where it answers, and a question with the one recommended answer only where the code's own say contradicts itself.

## Write Empty only when you cannot fill

**Default:** An `Empty` record says what stopped you, and you write it only when you could not fill the field and it is not a question.

**When:** A field that is neither a value nor a question.

Bad: `Empty: no time` on a field a source answers, where the filler would have read the source.
Good: `Empty: the route is built behind a flag I cannot read from the repo, and the flag's default is not in the tree`, on the field that is genuinely unfillable.

## List the script's missed rows, add none

**Law:** A thing in what the rows are read from that should be a row, that no row holds, and that the row script's stderr does not name as left out, is a defect in the script, a finding for the user: don't add a row for it — list it, with what it is read from, and the file and the quote that shows it.

**When:** Your read of what the rows are read from, for your slice.

Bad: A new row the filler wrote for the miss, so the table grows by hand.
Good: The miss in the report's Defects in the script list, with the file and the quote, and the table untouched.

## Run the parity gate before you report

**Law:** Before you report, run the gate on your slice — `node <this skill's folder>/scripts/ledger.mjs check <case> fill <slice>` — and fix your records until it exits 0.

**When:** The end of your fill, before the report.

The gate checks, on `<slice>/fill-fields.jsonl`: the file exists; every record has an `Id` and a `Field` and exactly one shape; every `Id` is a row of the slice and every `Field` is a field the fill holds as null on that row; no (`Id`, `Field`) is there twice; every row of the slice that is not struck and has no confirmed `CantHappen` has a record for every fill field other than `CantHappen` and `Shortfall`, unless the table already holds a value for it, or a question that has no ruling yet; every value has a citation, its file is under the root and exists (a `meridian:` file is a `rules-*.md` file in this skill's `references/` folder), and its quote is 3 characters or more and is in the file; every value of an expected field has a `Source` that is one of the five words, and its citations fit it (`written`: a file that is not the row script, not the file the row's `Where` names, and not a file under the case folder; `ruling`: a rulings file, the top-level `rulings.md` or your slice's; `meridian`: a `meridian:<rules-*.md>` cite whose quote is in that file; `judgement`: a non-empty `Why`); `CantHappen` and `Shortfall` records are values; a question has a `Question` and a `Recommend`; and an `Empty` says what stopped you.

Bad: A report sent with the gate at exit 1, and the fix "for next time".
Good: The gate at exit 0 before the report, with the records it refused fixed and re-run.

## Report every section, keyed by row id

**Preference:** Your report is facts only — what you read, the citation, what the code does — with no recommendations, no options, and no asks, and every claim carries a citation that greps, there being no second tier of claim; it goes at the report path your brief gives, under the case's `reports/`, each bullet keyed by row id at line start so `grep -rn <id> reports/` is the join, and it holds these sections: first line, how many rows of your slice you were given, how many fields you filled as a value, as a question, and as empty, and the `check` you ran with its exit code; **Rows**, every row by id at line start, with each field you filled — its value or question, and its citation — and then "today:", where the code does something the row's expected value does not say; **Can't happen**, the row id and why, with a citation on every link of the chain; **Shortfalls**, the row id, what the code does, and the citation; **Questions for the user**, the row id, the field, the question, and the one recommended answer; **Disagreements**, each place the code and a written source, a ruling, or a Meridian rule disagree, both cited; **Defects in the script**, each thing the script should have written as a row and did not, with the file and the quote that shows it; **Expected from today's code**, each expected value whose `Source` is `today`, by row id and field; **No source**, each row where nothing in the source order says what is expected; and **Not read**.

**When:** Every report you write.

Bad: A report whose bullets are keyed by field name, so `grep -rn <id> reports/` finds nothing, and whose one claim of note is "I think the row is fine".
Good: The same report keyed by row id at line start, every section present, even the empty ones, every claim a file and a quote you read around.

## Say what you did not read

**Preference:** Say what you did not read, in your report's "Not read" section.

**When:** The end of your fill.

Bad: A report that is silent about the two config files it never opened.
Good: The same report with "Not read: the two config files" and the reason, so the disprover knows the ground.

## Write the fill file with your file tool, the report by heredoc

**Preference:** Write `<slice>/fill-fields.jsonl` with your file tool as JSONL, one record per line; save the report with a shell heredoc to the report path your brief gives, not a file-writing tool; and reply with only the report path.

**When:** The end of your fill.

Bad: The report written with the file tool, so the session's heredoc convention and its review don't apply to it.
Good: The fill file by file tool, the report by heredoc under the case's `reports/`, and the reply that is only the path.
